office: U.S. Senate (special election, unexpired term ending January 2029)
scope_plain: Every Florida voter. This is a special election to finish the term Marco Rubio left when he became U.S. Secretary of State in January 2025. The winner serves through January 3, 2029, then faces a regular election in 2028. Write-in candidates do not appear by name; the ballot has a blank write-in line.
office_explainer: One of Florida's two senators in Washington. Votes on federal laws, budgets, treaties and judges.
why_it_matters: Senators confirm federal judges and cabinet members and vote on national taxes, health care, immigration and spending. Ashley Moody was appointed, not elected, so this is the first time voters weigh in on the seat since 2022.

candidates.name: Ashley Moody
candidates.background: Appointed to the U.S. Senate by Gov. DeSantis in January 2025 to replace Marco Rubio. Florida Attorney General 2019 to 2025; before that a Hillsborough County circuit judge and federal prosecutor. Won the Aug 18 Republican primary with 79.6%.

own_words.text: "The top three issues are the economy, public safety, and restoring trust and accountability to Washington."
"I am working to eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse so every taxpayer dollar is spent wisely."

candidates.name: Angie Nixon
candidates.background: State representative for House District 13 (Jacksonville) since 2020. Community organizer before the Legislature. Won the Aug 18 Democratic primary over Alex Vindman, 56.1% to 43.9%.

own_words.text: "Floridians are being crushed by an affordability crisis created by greed and corruption."
"I will fight to make childcare affordable and accessible."

candidates.name: Neil J. Gillespie
candidates.background: No-party candidate. Did not respond to the News4JAX questionnaire; no campaign website found.

own_words.text: Did not respond to the News4JAX candidate questionnaire.
No campaign website or platform statement found in this run.

scope_plain: Every Florida voter. Governor and lieutenant governor run as one ticket; you vote once for the pair. Open seat: Ron DeSantis is term-limited. The ballot lists 2 major-party tickets, 1 Libertarian ticket and 5 no-party (NPA) candidates, plus a write-in line (5 write-ins qualified; their names are not printed). Primary results: Donalds won the Republican primary with 47.8% over Lt. Gov. Jay Collins (25.2%); Jolly won the Democratic primary with 60.9%. Jerry Demings and Jason Pizzo, mentioned in earlier drafts, are NOT on the ballot.
office_explainer: Runs the state's executive branch: signs or vetoes laws, proposes the budget, appoints judges and agency heads.
why_it_matters: Four-year term. The governor appoints Florida Supreme Court justices and hundreds of board members, directs hurricane and emergency response, and sets the agenda on property insurance, schools, growth and taxes. First open-seat governor race since 2018.

candidates.name: Byron Donalds (Lt. Gov.: Bryan Avila)
candidates.background: U.S. representative for Florida's 19th District (Naples and Fort Myers) since 2021; Florida House 2016 to 2020; background in insurance and banking. Endorsed by President Trump in February 2025. Running mate Bryan Avila is a state senator from Miami-Dade, named Aug 25, 2026.

own_words.text: "Florida cannot become too expensive for working families and seniors on fixed incomes."
"We must secure our borders, keep local neighborhoods safe."
Education plank: "Every student should Read to Succeed, stay active and healthy, and have a debt-free route to a great-paying job."

candidates.name: David Jolly (Lt. Gov.: Gwen Graham)
candidates.background: Former Republican U.S. representative for Pinellas County (2014 to 2017) who left the GOP in 2018 and registered as a Democrat in 2025; MSNBC commentator. Running mate Gwen Graham is a former U.S. representative for North Florida and daughter of the late Gov. Bob Graham.

own_words.text: On home insurance: "Here is the plan to cut them by 60 to 70 percent."
"We can't move forward together if we are constantly being driven apart."
Economy: "everyone deserves a shot at work, wages, and wealth." Site also lists housing, healthcare, education and 'no data centers.'

scope_plain: Every Florida voter. One of three elected Cabinet seats that, with the governor, make up the Florida Cabinet. Two candidates; both were unopposed in their primaries.
office_explainer: Florida's top lawyer. Defends state laws in court, runs consumer protection, and sits on the Cabinet.
why_it_matters: Decides which lawsuits Florida files and joins, from immigration to tech regulation, and defends state laws when they are challenged. James Uthmeier was appointed, not elected, so this is voters' first say on him.

candidates.name: James Uthmeier
candidates.background: Appointed attorney general by Gov. DeSantis in February 2025 when Ashley Moody went to the U.S. Senate. Previously DeSantis's chief of staff and general counsel. Georgetown Law. Did not respond to the News4JAX questionnaire.

own_words.text: "James is focused on keeping Florida safe, strong, and free."
Lists "prosecuting dangerous criminals to combatting illegal immigration" and suing corporations he says are "sexualizing and indoctrinating our children."

candidates.name: Jose Javier Rodriguez
candidates.background: Workers' rights attorney; former state senator (2016 to 2020) and state representative from Miami-Dade; Assistant Secretary of Labor in the Biden administration. Harvard Law.

own_words.text: "The top three issues are crime, costs and corruption."
"I hope to be remembered for restoring the Attorney General's office to its core mission."

office: Florida Supreme Court: retain Chief Justice Carlos G. Muñiz?
scope_plain: Every Florida voter. Yes/no question. Muñiz is the only Supreme Court justice on the 2026 ballot (retained in 2020; justices face voters every six years). Florida has no official judicial performance commission, and The Florida Bar discontinued its lawyer retention poll in 2023, so there is no 2026 rating. No Florida appellate judge has ever lost a retention vote.
office_explainer: Highest state court. Final say on Florida law. Vote yes to keep the justice, no to remove.
why_it_matters: The seven justices decide what the Florida Constitution means, including on abortion, redistricting, ballot amendments and the death penalty. If a justice is not retained, the governor appoints a replacement.

candidates.name: Carlos G. Muñiz
candidates.background: Chief Justice since 2022 (re-elected by his peers 2024); on the court since January 2019, appointed by Gov. DeSantis. Before that: general counsel of the U.S. Department of Education, deputy attorney general under Pam Bondi, deputy general counsel to Gov. Jeb Bush. Yale Law 1997, UVA 1991.

own_words.text: Notable opinions: joined the 6-1 majority in Planned Parenthood v. State (April 2024) holding the state privacy clause does not protect abortion; wrote the July 2025 opinion upholding the DeSantis congressional map; in Conage directed courts to consider "all textual and structural clues" when reading statutes.
Official court biography.

office: First District Court of Appeal: retain Judge Joseph Lewis, Jr.?
district: 1st DCA (Panhandle and North Florida: Escambia, Santa Rosa, Okaloosa, Walton, Leon, Gadsden, Bay and 25 other counties)
scope_plain: Only voters in the First District see this. Tallahassee (Leon) and Pensacola (Escambia) are in the 1st DCA. Orlando is NOT: Orange County is in the 6th DCA, and no 6th DCA judges are up in 2026, so Orlando voters see no DCA questions this year.
office_explainer: Mid-level appeals court for the Panhandle and North Florida. Vote yes to keep the judge, no to remove.
why_it_matters: District courts of appeal are the final stop for most Florida appeals; the Supreme Court takes only a small share. The 1st DCA also hears many cases against state agencies because it sits in Tallahassee.

candidates.name: Joseph Lewis, Jr.
candidates.background: On the 1st DCA since 2001 (appointed by Gov. Jeb Bush). The court's longest-serving judge. Last retained in 2020 with 84% of responding lawyers recommending retention in the Bar's final poll.

own_words.text: No 2026 performance rating exists; The Florida Bar ended its retention poll in 2023. See the court biography.
